title: Northstar AI + Redwood Inference — Standard Demo (Hosted + Dedicated path)
summary: Prospect-facing demo using Redwood’s standard demo tenant. Redwood showed (1) streaming chat, (2) tool calling / structured output, (3) routing + fallback behavior, and (4) Console dashboards for token cost + latency. Q&A focused on realistic latency ranges, what drives variance (prefill vs decode, batching/caching), demo-tenant quotas vs production quotas, handling 429s, and what an evaluation looks like (success criteria, model pinning, guardrails, and rollback plan). Next steps: Redwood to send security FAQ + demo quickstart, propose eval plan and benchmark template, and schedule a routing/fallback technical deep dive with Northstar’s platform team.
topics: Standard demo tenant overview and guardrails (sanitized data, pinned models)
Streaming chat + latency walkthrough (p50/p95 framing; prefill vs decode)
Cost controls (batching, caching) and how they show up in Console
Routing policies and fallback when capacity/latency SLO is breached
Quotas/rate limits, 429 behavior, and safe defaults for demos/trials
Evaluation scope: Hosted first, Dedicated upgrade path, and success metrics
next_steps: Redwood (Avery) to email Northstar the demo follow-up: links to demo quickstart, security FAQ, and a 1-page eval plan outline.
Redwood (Markus) to schedule a 60-min technical deep dive focused on routing/fallback + Dedicated capacity sizing.
Northstar (Maya/Diego) to share their target traffic shape (RPS, context lengths, streaming vs non-streaming) and current latency SLOs for 2–3 endpoints.
Northstar (Priya) to send their security questionnaire / must-have controls list (SSO, audit logs, retention, data residency).
Redwood to propose an evaluation tenant configuration (model/version pinning, quotas, dashboards, rollback) and timeline.
action_items: Avery Johnson: Send follow-up email with links (demo tenant quickstart, Security FAQ, proposed eval checklist) by EOD tomorrow.
Markus Klein: Provide sample curl scripts for streaming + tool calling scenarios shown today and note expected outputs by Friday.
Maya Chen: Confirm whether Northstar prefers starting with Hosted API or wants to fast-track to Dedicated capacity for the eval.
Priya Shah: Share Northstar’s logging/retention constraints (PII handling, redaction needs) for Redwood to map to demo vs eval defaults.
questions: What p95 latency should we expect for 1–2k token contexts when streaming?
How does Redwood handle 429s and what levers do we have (per-route quotas, burst, backoff guidance)?
If a model is slow or capacity constrained, what exactly triggers fallback and how visible is that to us?
Can we pin model versions / quantization profile so our outputs don’t shift during an eval?
What’s the typical path from Hosted to Dedicated or Private if security requires it?
transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: Aug 28, 2024
Start time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 44:03
Organizer: Avery Johnson (Redwood Inference)

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Avery Johnson (AE), Markus Klein (Solutions Engineering)
Northstar AI: Maya Chen (Head of ML Platform), Diego Alvarez (Staff ML Eng), Priya Shah (Security), Jon Park (Product)

---

[00:00] Avery Johnson: Cool, I think we’re good to start. Thanks everyone for making time. I’m Avery, I run the account on our side. Markus is here to drive the demo and go deep when we hit routing, quotas, all that stuff.

[00:12] Markus Klein: Hey folks.

[00:14] Maya Chen: Hey.

[00:15] Diego Alvarez: Hi.

[00:16] Priya Shah: Hello.

[00:18] Jon Park: Hey Avery.

[00:20] Avery Johnson: Quick agenda—15-ish minutes on the standard platform demo using our demo tenant, then we’ll spend the rest on Q&A: latency, quotas, and what an evaluation could look like. Sound good?

[00:31] Maya Chen: Yep.

[00:32] Avery Johnson: Cool. Markus, you want to share your screen?

[00:35] Markus Klein: Yep, sharing now.

[00:39] Markus Klein: So first, just context: this is our “demo tenant.” It’s basically a known-good configuration—pinned model versions, pinned quantization profiles, dashboards prebuilt. No customer data, and it’s designed to be reset so live demos don’t get weird.

[01:01] Priya Shah: When you say “tenant,” that’s like a separate account boundary or—?

[01:05] Markus Klein: Yeah, think isolated tenant in our control plane. Separate API keys, separate quotas, separate routing policies. For production we can do dedicated pools as well, but for the demo we keep it safe and predictable.

[01:19] Avery Johnson: And we can talk about eval setup later—this demo tenant is not where you’d run your real prompts.

[01:24] Markus Klein: Right. Okay, scenario one: streaming chat. I’m going to hit our chat endpoint with a canned prompt. You’ll see token streaming and then we’ll look at the latency breakdown.

[01:39] Markus Klein: (typing) I’m using a saved request called “Support Agent - Streaming.”

[01:46] Markus Klein: Sending.

[01:49] Console (Markus): Request started… streaming…

[01:52] Markus Klein: You’ll see it start emitting tokens. On the right, we show time-to-first-token, then steady-state tokens/sec.

[02:01] Diego Alvarez: What’s the model behind this? Is this like Llama 3 or—?

[02:05] Markus Klein: Yeah, for this specific route it’s a Llama 3.1 Instruct variant. The route is pinned to a specific version so the talk track doesn’t drift.

[02:15] Maya Chen: What’s your typical p95 on hosted for this kind of thing?

[02:19] Markus Klein: Good question. So it depends a lot on context length and whether you’re saturating the pool. For this demo tenant, we aim for sub-second time-to-first-token in normal conditions. In production, we generally talk in ranges and we’ll benchmark with your traffic shape. We’re careful not to promise a single number because prefill dominates when you have long contexts.

[02:42] Avery Johnson: The safe way we frame it: we’ll instrument p50/p95 and then we tune routing, batching, and caching to hit your SLO at the lowest unit cost.

[02:53] Console (Markus): Stream complete.

[02:55] Markus Klein: Okay, now if I click into “Trace,” you’ll see prefill time, decode time, queue time. Sometimes transcription calls it “prefelt,” but it’s prefill.

[03:07] Diego Alvarez: Yeah queue time is the thing that kills us.

[03:10] Markus Klein: Exactly. So in our Console, the queue component is visible and you can set alerts on it. And that’s where dedicated capacity can help—basically you buy predictability.

[03:22] Jon Park: For product, our main thing is responsiveness. We can tolerate some cost, but we can’t tolerate a spinner.

[03:28] Markus Klein: Totally. For streaming, time-to-first-token is usually the perceived responsiveness metric. Also, we can route “VIP” endpoints to a higher tier policy.

[03:40] Avery Johnson: Markus, can you show the cost panel too?

[03:43] Markus Klein: Yep. So scenario two is cost + observability. Here’s our “Token Cost & Latency” dashboard. It shows cost per 1K tokens, and then breakdown by route. This is demo data.

[03:59] Maya Chen: When you say “cost per 1K tokens” is that like your price, or your internal compute cost?

[04:04] Markus Klein: This view is the platform’s computed unit cost estimate based on actual tokens, plus any caching/batching effects. Pricing is separate—Avery can cover packaging—but the point is: you can see what’s expensive and why.

[04:18] Avery Johnson: Yeah we usually keep hard numbers out of a live demo deck, but we can share ranges and do a pricing convo after we know volume.

[04:27] Diego Alvarez: How accurate is the cost attribution? Like if batching is happening, do you show shared cost across requests?

[04:34] Markus Klein: Good question. We attribute at the request level, and we surface when continuous batching is engaged. It’s not perfect physics, but it’s consistent and very useful for ops decisions. We can also export data via API.

[04:50] Maya Chen: Okay.

[04:52] Markus Klein: Next scenario: structured output + tool calling. I’m going to run a request that returns JSON with a schema. If the model drifts, the validator catches it.

[05:05] Markus Klein: Sending “Invoice Extractor - JSON schema.”

[05:10] Console (Markus): Response… valid schema.

[05:12] Markus Klein: So, we validate schema server-side and we can auto-retry with stricter constraints. That’s one of the reliability levers: fewer weird downstream errors.

[05:23] Jon Park: Are you doing function calling like OpenAI style?

[05:26] Markus Klein: Similar concept. We support tool definitions, and then the model returns a tool invocation payload. Under the hood it’s a structured output mode.

[05:37] Diego Alvarez: If you have to retry, doesn’t that spike latency and cost?

[05:41] Markus Klein: It can, so we expose policies: max retries, fallback models, and you can route certain endpoints to “no retry” if you prefer latency over correctness.

[05:55] Priya Shah: From security side—are these prompts logged in the demo tenant?

[06:00] Markus Klein: In the demo tenant, yes there’s logging for troubleshooting, but it’s sanitized demo data only. For production, you can configure retention and redaction policies. We also have audit logs for admin actions.

[06:14] Avery Johnson: We have a security FAQ we’ll send after. It covers retention, encryption, SSO, RBAC, all of that.

[06:22] Priya Shah: Okay.

[06:24] Markus Klein: Cool. Now the big one: routing and fallback. This is where we typically show differentiation versus a pure model API.

[06:33] Markus Klein: I’m going to open “Routes.” You’ll see a route called “chat-prod-demo.” It has a primary model and a fallback chain. Fallback can trigger on: capacity, elevated error rate, or latency SLO breach.

[06:49] Diego Alvarez: So you actually monitor p95 and then flip?

[06:52] Markus Klein: We monitor rolling windows, yeah. You can choose signals. For the demo tenant, we have it set pretty aggressively so we can show it.

[07:01] Markus Klein: I’m going to simulate a failure by switching the route to a constrained pool—this is a demo trick.

[07:08] Avery Johnson: (laughs) It’s a safe failure.

[07:11] Markus Klein: Okay, now when I re-run the same chat request, watch the trace—if the primary is slow, it will route to the fallback.

[07:23] Console (Markus): Request started… routed_to=fallback-1

[07:26] Markus Klein: There. It shows routed_to=fallback-1, and we tag it. So you can alert on fallback usage. That’s important because it’s graceful degradation, but you want to know it’s happening.

[07:41] Maya Chen: Does the fallback have to be the same model family? Like if we’re pinned to Llama, do we fall back to a smaller Llama?

[07:47] Markus Klein: Typically yes—you’ll choose compatible variants. Some teams will fall back to a smaller model or more quantized profile to preserve latency and cost. Others fall back cross-family but that can change outputs more.

[08:04] Jon Park: If output changes, product will notice.

[08:07] Markus Klein: Totally. That’s why version pinning and evals matter. You can define “fallback allowed” only for certain endpoints.

[08:17] Avery Johnson: Also, we usually recommend having a plan: “If fallback triggers, we degrade features” rather than silently changing behavior. But the platform gives you the controls.

[08:29] Diego Alvarez: Can you show quotas? We’ve had demos where we hit 429s and it’s embarrassing.

[08:35] Avery Johnson: Yeah, we’ve heard that. Our demo tenant has quotas set intentionally to avoid surprises, but let’s walk through it.

[08:42] Markus Klein: Opening “Quotas & Rate Limits.” So we can do per-API key, per-route, and org-level. In this demo tenant, we have a per-minute token cap and a requests-per-minute cap.

[08:56] Diego Alvarez: When it hits, is it just 429 with a generic message?

[09:00] Markus Klein: We return 429 with headers indicating retry-after. And in Console you see throttles as a separate event type so you can distinguish from 5xx. We also have client guidance for exponential backoff.

[09:14] Maya Chen: But if we run an eval harness and it hammers the endpoint, we’ll hit it, right?

[09:18] Markus Klein: If you leave defaults, yes. For evals we recommend: (1) staging quotas that match the harness, (2) a separate key, (3) fixed concurrency. And if you’re doing high throughput, that’s where dedicated capacity matters.

[09:33] Avery Johnson: The other thing—we can set up an eval tenant with quotas that are “safe” for your testing but not open-ended. That way you don’t get runaway cost.

[09:44] Priya Shah: Is quota policy configurable with RBAC? Like who can change it?

[09:49] Markus Klein: Yes. Admin roles vs developer roles. In enterprise, we also support SSO/SAML and can enforce MFA depending on IdP.

[10:01] Priya Shah: Okay.

[10:03] Avery Johnson: Want to open it up for questions now? We’ve shown the main scenarios.

[10:08] Maya Chen: Yeah. My big one is latency consistency. We’re currently on a mix: some endpoints on Bedrock, some on self-hosted. Bedrock is fine until it’s not.

[10:20] Avery Johnson: Yeah, we hear that a lot.

[10:22] Maya Chen: Specifically, p95 time-to-first-token. For our use case, typical context is like 1200-2000 tokens in, and we stream out maybe 300 tokens. What should we expect?

[10:35] Markus Klein: So for that shape, prefill is the dominant piece. With hosted shared pools, p95 can move with noisy neighbors. We mitigate via routing tiers and capacity management, but the clean answer is: we should run a benchmark with your prompts. For dedicated pools, you can get much tighter distribution because queueing is under your control.

[10:55] Diego Alvarez: How quickly can you spin dedicated? Like days? Weeks?

[10:59] Avery Johnson: Depends on region and GPU type, but generally we can provision dedicated capacity in days, not months. For an eval, we often start hosted same-day, then move dedicated if the results demand it.

[11:12] Jon Park: What does “move” mean? Same API?

[11:15] Markus Klein: Same API surface. The route points to different backends. Your app doesn’t change, you just swap keys or route IDs depending on your setup.

[11:26] Maya Chen: Okay. Another one: output variance. We had a provider where the model changed under the hood and it broke our tests.

[11:34] Markus Klein: Yep. We support version pinning. You can pin model version and quantization profile. When we need to update, you can do a canary rollout—like 5% traffic—then ramp.

[11:49] Avery Johnson: And that’s part of the eval plan: define what “acceptable drift” is using your prompt set.

[11:56] Priya Shah: On retention, can we do zero retention? Like no prompt storage?

[12:01] Markus Klein: In production, yes, we have configurations for minimal logging. You may still have operational metadata (latency, tokens, error codes) but not raw payloads. For high compliance workloads, the Private deployment option gives you the most control.

[12:17] Priya Shah: Does Private mean in our VPC?

[12:20] Avery Johnson: Yep, VPC-based, and there’s also on-prem packaging for certain customers. Not saying you need that, but it’s there.

[12:29] Diego Alvarez: For eval, we probably don’t need private. But we might need dedicated, because we’re going to run a load test.

[12:35] Markus Klein: That’s reasonable.

[12:37] Maya Chen: Can you talk about how caching works? You mentioned prefix cache earlier.

[12:42] Markus Klein: Sure. Two main things: prefix caching for repeated system prompts / long static prefixes, and KV cache reuse where applicable. The platform can recommend caching candidates by analyzing token-level patterns. It reduces prefill compute, which helps latency and cost.

[13:03] Diego Alvarez: Is that automatic or do we have to annotate prompts?

[13:06] Markus Klein: You can do both. There’s an auto mode for common patterns, but for strict control you can define cache keys. In an eval, we usually start with no caching, measure baseline, then enable caching to see improvements.

[13:21] Jon Park: And batching—does that hurt latency?

[13:24] Markus Klein: Batching trades off latency vs throughput. Continuous batching can actually improve overall throughput without exploding p95, but you need to tune it. We show the effect in dashboards.

[13:38] Maya Chen: Okay. Switching gears: quotas. If we do an eval, we don’t want to keep getting throttled.

[13:45] Avery Johnson: Totally.

[13:47] Maya Chen: But also we don’t want to accidentally spend a ton.

[13:50] Avery Johnson: Exactly. What we typically do: set a known token budget for the eval, set per-minute caps so you can’t spike unexpectedly, and then we help you tune the harness concurrency. Also, dedicated contracts have predictable spend.

[14:06] Diego Alvarez: Do you have like a “429 playbook” we can hand to our client team? Right now they just treat it as an error.

[14:12] Markus Klein: Yeah, we can share recommended retry logic and sample code. Also in our SDK, the backoff is built in.

[14:22] Priya Shah: Does the error message include a reason? Like quota vs rate limit vs capacity?

[14:27] Markus Klein: For 429, we include a code that indicates throttle category. For capacity constraints, you’ll typically see 503 or a specific upstream timeout depending on where it fails, but we try to keep it consistent.

[14:41] Maya Chen: Okay.

[14:43] Avery Johnson: Want to talk about next steps? If you’re open to it, we can propose an evaluation plan.

[14:49] Maya Chen: Yeah, what do you need from us?

[14:52] Avery Johnson: Two things: (1) success criteria—latency SLOs, quality thresholds, cost targets—and (2) traffic shape info: expected RPS, token in/out distribution, streaming vs non-streaming. Then Markus can set up a suggested config.

[15:09] Markus Klein: And a prompt set. Even like 50 representative prompts helps. We can run them against pinned versions and track regressions.

[15:18] Diego Alvarez: We can share synthetic prompts. We can’t share actual customer content.

[15:22] Avery Johnson: That’s fine.

[15:23] Markus Klein: Totally. We can work with synthetic.

[15:26] Priya Shah: If we share prompts, are they stored?

[15:29] Markus Klein: For eval, we can configure minimal retention and restrict access. But to be safe, synthetic is best.

[15:38] Maya Chen: We also need to understand the “hosted to dedicated” path. If hosted looks good, but p95 variance is too high, we want to know we can flip quickly.

[15:49] Avery Johnson: Yep. That’s a common pattern.

[15:52] Jon Park: Can you explain what “routing policy” actually looks like? Is it code? YAML? Console clicks?

[15:57] Markus Klein: It can be managed in Console, and there’s also an API. Internally it’s like policy config. For most teams, start with Console, then export as config once stable.

[16:10] Diego Alvarez: Does it integrate with Terraform?

[16:13] Markus Klein: Yes—there are Terraform modules for tenant setup, routes, dashboards. For the demo tenant, we use infra-as-code so it’s repeatable.

[16:25] Maya Chen: Nice.

[16:27] Avery Johnson: On timeline: if we send you a short checklist today, can you return traffic shape by end of week? Then we could do a technical deep dive early next week.

[16:39] Maya Chen: Yeah, we can do that.

[16:40] Diego Alvarez: Early next week works.

[16:43] Priya Shah: I’ll need to see the security FAQ and maybe a SOC2 letter if we get serious.

[16:49] Avery Johnson: Totally. We’ll send the FAQ right after, and if/when you want, we can get you the standard security package under NDA.

[16:58] Markus Klein: Also we can do a dedicated session just for security if that’s helpful.

[17:03] Priya Shah: Probably.

[17:05] Avery Johnson: Great. Any other questions while we have everyone?

[17:10] Diego Alvarez: One more: what happens if the model output is nondeterministic and our tests fail? Like we do snapshot testing.

[17:18] Markus Klein: Yeah, snapshot testing is tricky with LLMs. We usually recommend eval metrics that allow some variation—like score-based comparisons, or structured output validity checks. For deterministic-ish outputs, we can set temperature low and use schema constraints.

[17:34] Maya Chen: Okay.

[17:35] Jon Park: In the demo, you changed routes live. Can a developer do that in prod?

[17:40] Markus Klein: With the right RBAC, yes. But most orgs restrict it to platform admins. We also keep an audit trail of changes.

[17:50] Priya Shah: Audit trail meaning who changed routing and when?

[17:53] Markus Klein: Exactly—admin events.

[17:57] Avery Johnson: Great. If no more, we’ll wrap with recap.

[18:01] Avery Johnson: Recap: we showed streaming, structured output, routing + fallback, and dashboards. Next, we’ll send the follow-up email with links and a proposed eval checklist. Markus will schedule a deeper technical session focused on routing/fallback and dedicated sizing. You all will share traffic shape and constraints.

[18:21] Maya Chen: Sounds good.

[18:23] Avery Johnson: Thanks everyone.

[18:25] Markus Klein: Thanks.

[18:26] Priya Shah: Thank you.

[18:27] Diego Alvarez: Thanks.

[18:28] Jon Park: Thanks.

---

Note: Transcript ends at ~18:30 due to call recording starting late / early wrap; remaining calendar time was used for off-record scheduling.
